## TL;DR

Addressed the four concrete review findings in the parallel close-out pipeline. Publish work no longer consumes a validation slot, cooled jobs do not reserve capacity, and queue status only calls the actual publish head active. Main checkout bookkeeping now uses the shared locks, and a failed attempt to restore review state schedules a retry instead of silently abandoning the repair or blocking a run indefinitely. Corrected the documentation for parked validation budgets.

## Work and rationale

The scheduler has two distinct kinds of work: validations that can overlap, and publishing that must serialize. The start selector previously incremented its in-flight count when it selected the publish head. That treated a publisher as a validation and left an available runner slot unused. Publishing now remains independently selectable while the validation counter only tracks validation work. The selector accepts an unavailable set for cooldown state; it scans past those jobs but still preserves the queue head for publish-order decisions. Cancelled jobs remain eligible for teardown even when capacity is full or a job is cooling.

The scheduler now passes cooling job IDs into the selector, rather than selecting them and discarding them afterward. This lets later validations use free slots while a crashed head waits out backoff. The selector still determines publish turn from the complete queue, so this does not allow later jobs to publish early. The existing pressure guard remains applied to additional validation work.

Pipeline status previously chose the first started job as active. If the queue head had crashed and was cooling, a later runner could be presented as the active head and named as the blocker for the true head. The read model now assigns `active` only when the queue head is executing. Other executing jobs remain in the parallel list, and the unstarted head remains queued without a misleading blocker. Regression coverage exercises this cooling-head snapshot.

The release stamp and optional dirty-worktree marker are written in cleanup, after `publishCandidate` has released its main checkout locks. These writes now acquire the same repository and root locks around the task-file mutation. Failure recovery also restores worktree review protection and review status while holding those locks. If the locks remain busy, it retries asynchronously after a short bounded attempt; this prevents restoration from being permanently skipped and avoids making the close-out execution wait forever. The release stamp retries until it obtains the locks because a successfully published task must be marked released.

Updated `docs/close-out-pipeline.md` to state that time parked for the publish turn is excluded, while the validation budget already spent remains charged. The attempt budget is shifted by parked duration and does not reset.

## Approaches tried

I first tried making checkout-lock acquisition unbounded so that recovery could never skip restoration. The required check exposed why this was wrong: a test deliberately holds the main lock, and an unbounded wait caused the test to hit its 120-second timeout. I replaced that approach with bounded waits and a delayed retry for failure restoration. The retry operates through the same lock helper and keeps the job's failure result available immediately.

I also tried invoking Vitest with the UI app's configuration and a server test path. That configuration only discovers tests under `src/ui-app/tests`, so it reported no server test files. I relied on the repository check for its configured suite and the direct tests were included in the branch's test changes, but I do not count the mis-targeted command as verification.

## Challenges and blockers

The configured Tailscale validation could not get a qualifying link probe on thinkpad, bee, or mini in either check. RepoOS fell back to the serialized local full gate. The first run passed build, format, lint, static safety checks and UI smoke, but the test step failed: its slowest reported case was the hotfix-lock test in `done-guard-orchestrator.test.ts`, which timed out after 120 seconds. This was caused by my first unbounded lock-wait implementation and led to the bounded asynchronous recovery retry described above.

The required check passed against the final checkpoint. RepoOS recorded `passed: true` with no failed steps; 624 test files passed (9,059 tests passed, one skipped), followed by UI smoke and the user-docs build. The local fallback waited about 95 seconds for its serialized slot in the prior run; this final run also used local fallback after all three runner link probes failed. Those host skips were network throughput failures, not test failures. The two focused regression test files passed independently as well (17 tests).

## Key learnings

Capacity should represent the resource being limited: a serialized publisher does not use a validation runner slot. A cooldown is scheduler state, not queue membership; it should prevent restarting one job without preventing independent work behind it. Status should describe the publish head separately from concurrent validation workers so a crash backoff does not transfer head identity to another task.

Finally, lock safety needs both ownership and liveness. Silently dropping a write after a timeout loses required state restoration, while waiting forever can deadlock tests and callers. Bounded acquisition with a durable retry path gives both safety and progress.
